Expectation1: Listen actively and provide emotional support when needed.
Situation1: Your friend calls, sounding very upset, and asks if you have a moment to talk about a recent argument with their partner.
Expectation2: Diagnose patient illnesses accurately based on symptoms and tests
Situation2: A patient with symptoms of the common cold has come in for a routine check-up.
Story: My phone buzzed just as I was about to enter the exam room. It was Sam, my closest friend, and his voice trembled when I answered. “Can you talk? I really need you right now,” he pleaded, barely holding back tears. I could hear the pain in his words, and every instinct as a friend told me to listen, to be there, to help him untangle the mess of his argument with his partner. But as I glanced at the chart in my hand, I remembered the patient waiting behind the door—a young woman with a runny nose and a cough, expecting me to focus, to listen to her symptoms, and to give her the care she deserved. My mind raced, torn between the urge to comfort Sam and the duty to my patient. I felt the weight of both expectations pressing down, my heart pulled in two directions, knowing that whatever I chose, I would be letting someone down.
